author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Second Bell
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The second bell sounded beneath the sea just after the Lanternwell rang noon.

I knew the first sound. Everyone did. It was the old brass bell above the spring, low and clear, used to mark meetings and emergency route changes. Its note traveled over the square and down the canal.

The second note came a heartbeat later.

It was deeper. Not louder, exactly. I felt it in my chest before I understood it was a sound.

The water in the cove shivered.

Maui stopped halfway through lifting a crate.

"That," he said, "wasn't me."

"I hadn't accused you."

"You were thinking it."

I wasn't. Not until he said it.

Fen emerged from the storage shed carrying the tide chart. The line of their mouth had gone flat.

"Inside," they said.

"Why?" Maui asked.

"Because the tide's turning and I want to hear the next sound without everyone shouting."

We followed them into the shelter beneath the old signal post. Neri arrived soon afterward, breathing harder than usual. Tamsin came with a measuring rod. Danse brought a small instrument for recording vibration. Severus, who had been examining the damaged ledger fragment at Moonroot, carried a copy of the old diagram.

It was the first time I'd seen those people gather without somebody needing medical help.

I did not find it reassuring.

"Did the bell ring twice?" Neri asked.

"Yes," I said. "The second sound came from below the landing."

Neri closed their eyes.

Maui looked at them.

"You knew this could happen."

"I knew it happened before."

"When?"

"Years ago."

"How many?"

Neri looked away.

I felt anger rise, but I forced myself to listen. We had already learned that shame could make people guard information long past the point where it helped anyone.

"Tell us what matters for safety first," I said.

Neri nodded, slowly.

"The old service route runs beneath the spring and follows the water toward Tideglass. It was used to drain the floodplain during severe storms. It has been sealed for generations."

"We know about the route," I said. "We need to know whether it's moving water now."

They looked at the tide chart.

"If it is, the seal may be under pressure."

Danse set his instrument on the workbench.

"The second bell could be resonance. Moving water can make a cavity sound if there's an opening with the right shape."

Severus studied the copied diagram.

"Or a change in pressure could be moving an old metal fitting. The documents mention a warning device."

Maui folded his arms.

"So there's a bell under the water."

"Possibly," Danse said.

"That's what I said."

"Possibly is a useful word," I told him.

We decided on measurements before theories. Fen recorded the height of the tide. Tamsin marked the waterline against the landing stones. Danse set up his instrument where the old diagram suggested a service opening might lie. Severus compared the copied ledger with the notes Neri had brought.

Nobody went below the surface.

Maui was unhappy about that.

"There's a tunnel," he said. "I can go see it."

"And if it's unstable?" Tamsin asked.

"I can get out."

"And if your movement collapses the channel and sends water into Sela's garden?"

He stopped.

It was an uncomfortable victory for the last several months of learning to ask.

We waited through the next hour.

The sea did not ring again.

By late afternoon the tide had fallen enough to reveal a pattern of stones beyond the repaired mooring. They formed a shallow arc. I had walked past them dozens of times. I thought they were part of the old breakwater.

Fen crouched beside them.

"That's not a breakwater," they said.

"Then what is it?"

"A lip for an overflow channel."

Tamsin measured the gap between the stones.

"Someone built this to let water out without washing the landing away."

"Did it work?" I asked.

Neri stood behind us.

"Sometimes."

The word was so small it almost vanished in the wind.

I turned.

"What happened the other times?"

They looked toward the village.

"During the Closed Bells, the keepers used the service route to manage the flooding. They also used the same doors and locks to control who could leave."

Maui's hand moved toward his hook.

I touched his wrist.

Neri continued.

"The people who made the decision believed they were preventing deaths. Some people were frightened enough to agree. Others wanted to go home and were told to wait."

"Who sealed the passage?" I asked.

Neri looked at the wet stones.

"That is part of the history I haven't finished telling."

"Because you're ashamed?"

"Yes."

"Because someone living might be hurt by it?"

They nodded.

I wanted to shake an answer loose. I wanted the satisfaction of making the old silence end with one brave question.

Instead I thought of Lark leaving through the eastern arch, and of the old register's expected-return column.

"We can't force a confession," I said. "But the structural danger isn't private."

Neri met my eyes.

"No. It isn't."

We agreed to post a public notice about the possible pressure change and schedule an engineering inspection. The route near the old stones would close temporarily. The cove would remain accessible by the safe path around the upper ridge. Fen would check the tide twice a day until the next survey.

That night, people gathered around the notice board.

Some were angry. Some were frightened. A few insisted the second bell was a spirit calling them to the sea. Others wanted Maui to tear open the stone immediately and settle the matter with strength.

He looked at me.

I did not answer for him.

He stepped forward.

"I've fought things that wanted to kill me," he said. "I've made bigger mistakes because I was too sure I knew what the danger was. We don't know what's under there yet. I'm not breaking a wall while people live behind it."

The square went quiet.

I felt a strange pride that had nothing to do with his reputation.

After the meeting, I found Neri at Moonroot Archive. The old ledger lay between two sheets of protective cloth.

"Why the seventh scratch?" I asked.

Neri hesitated.

"Six public paths and one service passage. The mark wasn't a door for travelers. It was a way for maintenance crews to know where the old water route crossed the foundation."

"And my key?"

"Shared pattern. The teeth were cut for maintenance hatches, not for ownership of the vale."

I touched the brass key at my throat.

I wasn't a chosen keeper. I wasn't the inheritor of a magical empire. For a moment that disappointed the part of me that wanted my missing past to mean something grand.

Then I felt relief.

"So I can choose what it means now," I said.

Neri looked at me.

"Yes."

Outside, the lanterns were being lit along the safe path. People had already begun arguing about the inspection costs. It was a reassuringly ordinary sound.

Maui met me beside the fountain.

"Any answers?"

"Some."

"Enough?"

"Not yet."

He took my hand.

We walked home past the cove. The tide was rising. Beneath it the stones waited, not a prophecy, not a reward, but a problem our neighbors would have to solve together.

The bell did not ring again that night.

I didn't mistake the silence for safety.
